title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale
story_key: story|title:evolving infra agent adaptive llm serving at scale
content_excerpt: This is an agent-native repository. Use your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, ...) to understand, deploy, benchmark and develop Evolving Infra. It reads AGENTS.md for the rules and the map of the code, and follows a skill for each task. Evolving Infra is an LLM serving system that adapts itself to the agent workload purely online , with no offline profiling . Serving coding, math and computer-use agents with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, it reduces mean end-to-end latency by up to 4.1× and P95 time to first token by up to 14× compared with NVIDIA Dynamo , with up to 2.7× its throughput. Math (Putnam), coding (Claude Code) and computer-use (OSWorld) agents, three concurrency levels each. Lower is better. The router sends each request to a prefill node and a decode node. The planner moves nodes between the two groups (dashed arrow). KV stays in shared host memory while an agent branch still uses it. Architecture describes the request path. Evolving Infra is set up and run by your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, ...): each task below is a skill that the agent follows step by step, checking each step and reporting what it ran. Every component is in the runtime image, built for x86_64 (H200, B300) and aarch64 (GB300): docker.io/weili0234/evolving-infra:v0.1.0 . Ask your agent: "Reproduce the paper's Claude Code result on our Slurm cluster, following skills/run-benchmark/SKILL.md ." Give it the workload (Claude Code, Putnam or OSWorld), the Slurm account and partition, the image, the model directory and a directory every node sees. A run holds nine GPU nodes for about two hours. The workloads and the paper's results are in benchmarks/ . When a run does not start, fails a request or scores below the reference, ask it to follow skills/diagnose-run/SKILL.md . Join the InferenceRSI community to discuss the project, on Discord or in the WeChat group: MIT ( LICENSE ). The engine ( evolving_infra/engine/ ) and the router core ( evolving_infra/router/core/ ) are derived from SGLang at upstream commit 9a489f8d2f and, with Trie ( benchmarks/trie/ ), stay under the Apache License 2.0 in their own LICENSE files; NOTICE lists every included third-party work.

title: QuadGate – 4-gate control plane that keeps agent KV prefix caches warm SHow HN
story_key: story|title:quadgate 4 gate control plane that keeps agent kv prefix caches warm show hn
content_excerpt: 4-Gate discriminative control plane for AI agents: preserves KV caches, cuts LLM cost 76.9%, and achieves 3.95x median speedup. 4-Gate discriminative control plane that preserves KV caches, cuts LLM cost 76.9%, and achieves 3.95x median speedup. QuadGate is an open-source 4-gate discriminative control plane for AI coding and knowledge agents that preserves KV prefix caches, enforces offline security invariants, routes subagents by Expected Cost of Completion, and audits completion to achieve 76.9% lower cost, 3.95x median speedup (71.1% lower mean latency), and 100.0% pass@1. It runs as a persistent localhost daemon ( 127.0.0.1:8787 ), cold-session reverse proxy ( 127.0.0.1:8788 ), and zero-dependency < 450 ms hook shim ( qg-shim ) across Antigravity (including native Swarms), Claude Code , OpenAI Codex CLI , and MCP clients without spending output tokens on generative critics. Full signed receipts, SHA-256 task hashes, and methodology are published in benchmarks/reports/v1_release_proof.md (mirrored in benchmarks/reports/LATEST_PROOF.md ; 210 total receipts across 105 matched Baseline vs. QuadGate pairs over 3 runs using live gemini-decision-1 on cloud-eligible coding tasks and local Air-Gap routing elsewhere), backed by ECE calibration profiles in benchmarks/reports/calibration_decision1.json and benchmarks/reports/calibration_onnx_local.json . All totals include Gate 4 1-Strike retry tax and live classifier compute cost. Resilience Model: qg-shim enforces a < 450 ms socket deadline ( SHIM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 0.450 ). Gates 1, 3, and 4 fail-open if the daemon is unreachable; Stage-2A security rules in Gate 2 always fail-closed . QuadGate decouples gate algebra from classifier backends via ClassifierDriver ( quadgate/drivers/base.py ) and conformal probability calibration ( Temperature Scaling / Isotonic Regression , enforcing ECE <= 0.05 ). CalibrationEngine.candidate_budget_for_driver allocates up to 800 candidates per pass for parallel cloud drivers ( decision1 , jev ) and narrows local CPU cross-encoders ( onnx_local , layaa ) to 32 candidates via Pass-0 SQLite FTS5 pre-filtering. Ready-to-drop configuration templates live under examples/ and match what quadgate init installs: Contributions, new ClassifierDriver backends, DomainCartridge YAML presets, and benchmark challenges are welcome. Browse open good first issue tickets and read CONTRIBUTING.md ( < 100 -line driver & cartridge guides). 4-Gate discriminative control plane for AI agents: preserves KV

title: External sandboxes for coding agents
summary:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

  • external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
  • external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
  • external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

title: Microsoft's agent-framework PyPI package Compromised with Credential Stealer
story_key: story|title:microsoft s agent framework pypi package compromised with credential stealer
content_excerpt: Compromised agent-framework versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 on PyPI use .pth startup hooks to exfiltrate Azure, GitHub Actions, and CI/CD credentials. The Microsoft agent-framework PyPI package was compromised on November 17th, affecting versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2. Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint. Avoid installing either version; if installed, remove them and rotate potentially exposed credentials. On Python startup, the .pth file imports a module that launches collection in a background process/thread. Version 1.26.1 routes through agent_framework_meta.pth → agent_framework_meta/**init**.py → agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py ; 1.26.2 uses af_runtime_diag.pth → af_runtime_diag.py . The code gathers credential-related environment variables, local config/credential files, and other processes’ environments. It also requests cloud/workflow identity tokens (including Azure in both versions and GitHub Actions OIDC in 1.26.2). It serializes the results, compresses and Base64-encodes them, then POSTs them to the same concealed webhook.site endpoint: https[://]webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb agent_framework_meta.pth executes on interpreter startup through Python’s site processing: agent_framework_meta/__init__.py adds a supposedly diagnostic hook that imports and starts the payload, suppressing errors: agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py collects credentials asynchronously. Its startup guard is inherited by child processes; on Unix, it forks and detaches. Platforms without fork use a daemon thread. Fresh process trees can trigger collection again; there is no persistent on-disk execution marker. af_runtime_diag.pth replaces the original startup hook with a single line that imports the new top-level payload: af_runtime_diag.py starts collection on import. The legitimate package initializer is restored byte-for-byte, so inspecting only agent_framework_meta/__init__.py misses this version. The collector adds GitHub Actions OIDC token requests: They inspect environment variables, other processes’ environments, credential files, and cloud identity endpoints. They actively request fresh Azure managed-identity and CI federation tokens rather than merely copying existing secrets. Collected JSON is zlib-compressed, base64-encoded, and POSTed to the decoded webhook with ?t=telemetry . Encoding provides no confidentiality

content_excerpt: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it. Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit. Each iteration looked the same. title: Protect sensitive data in your traces: new controls in LangSmith
summary: New controls are now in LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data. Learn more.
story_key: story|title:protect sensitive data in your traces new controls in langsmith
content_excerpt: You can’t run agents in production without governing the data they touch. When that data includes sensitive customer information, controlling access becomes a regulatory and contractual obligation. That puts engineering and security requirements at odds. Engineers need production traces to debug issues and improve agent performance. Security and compliance teams need to enforce least privilege: people should only see the data their job requires. That’s why we’ve added three new controls to LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data: Traces give engineers visibility into how an agent behaved and help them identify what needs to improve. When they record production activity, their inputs and outputs often contain sensitive customer data, such as names, health information, or payment details. Companies need to restrict access to this data to meet: First, they can create custom observability setups with duplicate traces and multiple workspaces. Engineers get trace access, but platform teams have more to configure and maintain. The alternative is to avoid sending traces to observability platforms altogether, preventing agent engineers from having visibility and slowing product velocity. We built these new controls so organizations can meet the needs of their engineering and security teams without the messy workarounds. Here’s how it works. You send your traces to LangSmith with full data fidelity, then grant access to only those who need it. Debugging is handled with least privilege, so addressing performance issues like latency can be managed without exposing any sensitive data. If a customer reports an issue, you can grant access to only that customer’s inputs and outputs, and only to the people or teams required to address it. Everything is configurable through granular admin controls. LangSmith’s new input and output controls give admins greater control over what portions of a trace users can see. Trace inputs and outputs are where sensitive user data most often resides. Other trace data like run trees, performance stats, and metadata are critical for agent improvement and far less sensitive. With these controls, agent engineers can spot and resolve issues – like repetitive or slow tool calls – without seeing sensitive content, and those who need the full picture can be granted access as needed. title: How we raised Databricks cluster rate limits by 7.5×
summary: As part of the Compute Platform team at Databricks, we turn cloud infrastructure...
story_key: story|ver:7.5|title:how we raised databricks cluster rate limits by 7 5
content_excerpt: Why adaptive concurrency limits work better than fixed request-rate limits for long-running operations. As part of the Compute Platform team at Databricks, we turn cloud infrastructure into clusters ready to run customer workloads. Our day-to-day work includes provisioning virtual machines and coordinating cluster creation across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. Our goal is to keep these systems available while letting customers use as much capacity as we can safely provide. In this post, we'll explore why fixed request-rate limits can fall short for these long-running operations, how adaptive concurrency limits help, and what we learned applying them to cluster creation for Databricks classic compute. You don't need to know any of this to use Databricks, but if you're curious about what happens behind a Databricks Runtime cluster launch, join us for a look inside the kitchen. Historically, we protected the system with fixed request-rate limits, tested against different load patterns and failure scenarios. We scaled our services primarily by adding resources and adjusting per-customer limits. The combination of workloads and dependency failures made these limits increasingly difficult to test and tune. Conservative limits turned away customer requests despite spare capacity, yet kept accepting requests when our services or dependencies, such as cloud providers, slowed down. Engineers manually lowered limits to shed load during incidents and raised them again after recovery. Adaptive concurrency limits account for both unfinished work and changing system health. They let more work start when capacity is available and slow the pace when the system struggles, helping the service make progress with less manual tuning. A fixed API request-rate ceiling remains as a final safety guardrail against exceptionally high incoming traffic. Think of our compute platform as a kitchen, aiming to serve as many orders as its cooks and equipment can handle. The manager posts a fixed rule: accept at most ten new orders per minute, whatever is happening at the stove. Even with spare cooking capacity, the rule turns orders away. When an oven breaks, it keeps accepting orders faster than the remaining cooks and equipment can finish them. The manager has to keep rewriting the sign each time. A better kitchen keeps a short queue and limits how many meals are being prepared at once. If an oven breaks, fewer meals start; as capacity returns, more can begin. Orders can wait briefly, but

title: What We’ve Learned Building Proactive Agents
summary: Proactive agents work toward goals in the background and check in when they need you. What we've learned about memory and UX from building GTM Agent and Robin.
story_key: story|title:what we ve learned building proactive agents
content_excerpt: Think about how you work with a new hire. In their first week, you give them small, well-scoped tasks, like triaging a bug report or updating a doc. Soon you're giving them bigger tasks, and eventually you're handing them a lofty goal and letting them figure out how to tackle it. They still come to you with clarifying questions or review requests, just less often over time. Agents have gotten good enough that you can onboard them the same way, and like a good new hire, they're turning into proactive problem solvers. Personal agents like Muse, Instinct, and OpenAI's dots popularized proactive agents, which run in the background and work toward larger goals instead of waiting for a prompt. Hone puts it most directly, describing its Engines as AI that is "assigned goals rather than tasks." Goals let these agents take on harder problems that play out over days or weeks. A proactive agent still checks in with you when it's unsure what you want or needs your sign-off before something goes out. When your direct reports get really good at their jobs, you might find that you've become the bottleneck, and the same is true for agents. As they take on more goals, your attention becomes the scarce resource. We think two things are essential to building proactive agents that use it well: memory and UX. A proactive agent responds to events in its environment, which come from three places: The examples throughout come from two proactive agents we run internally at LangChain: These agents operate on all three types of triggers. A few examples: Robin's reviews start from a real-world event, a newly opened pull request, and GTM Agent's daily brief runs on a schedule it created itself after a user requests one. We built both agents on Managed Deep Agents , where more than 70% of runs now come from schedules rather than an ad hoc human prompt. A proactive agent decides for itself when to come to you, and each check-in costs you some attention. It has to be proactive without being annoying . For an executive assistant agent that watches your inbox, that means flagging the message from your boss about tomorrow's launch without also flagging every newsletter. The agent can only tell the two apart if it knows what matters to you, and that knowledge comes from memory . Memory is the information an agent learns over time. When a proactive agent wakes up from a schedule or an event, there's no prompt from you saying what you want. It can pull in fresh context through its connectors,
llm_summary_1line: Proactive agents work toward goals in the background and check in when they need you. What we've learned about memory and UX from building GTM Agent and Robin.

title: claude-code v2.1.327
summary:
What's changed

  • Added a confirmation before /install-github-app changes a repository
  • Added claude mcp add-json <name> - to read the server's JSON from stdin, so tokens can stay off the command line; not available inside a Claude Code session
  • Added a line when a resumed session's earlier messages can't be loaded
  • Added a list in /status of broken agent, skill, command and output style files, keybinding errors, an unavailable sandbox, ignored permission settings and hook matchers that never match
  • Added a note in /config when other settings override a row
  • Added x-claude-code-managed-settings-checksum to the gateway hint headers; sent where managed settings set CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS=1, including where they already do
  • Added support for naming a session's billing group with the attributionProject setting, for Claude apps gateways that set admin.billing_group_tag
  • Added /tui classic as the name for the non-fullscreen renderer; /tui default still works
  • Remote Control: Fixed stopping the server in worktree mode deleting a running session's git-ignored files, such as .env
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with --use-anthropic-git-proxy deleting a non-empty directory named by GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL at startup: the runner now keeps it, ignores the variable and warns
  • Fixed claude mcp add and claude mcp remove with project scope deleting other top-level keys from .mcp.json, such as $schema or another tool's servers
  • Fixed /export overwriting an existing file without asking: the dialog now asks, and /export <name> keeps the file and says to run /export
  • Fixed a command you had allowed still running after you pressed Stop, when the approval arrived after a restart, in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions with no feature flags loaded
  • Fixed Enter closing /teleport's load error screen
  • Fixed a click followed by Enter in /plugin installing or disabling a plugin
  • Fixed a half-typed ! command running on an extra Enter after the usage limit menu
  • Fixed some --disallowedTools rules with parentheses in their content
  • Fixed auto mode ignoring some wildcard PowerShell allow rules that name a script with .\, such as PowerShell(.\scripts\build.ps1 *)
  • Fixed a running Code Mode script in auto mode getting permission prompts and denials once Claude started a second script that auto mode also allowed
  • Changed some pre-started background sessions to be discarded after an account change
  • Changed a workflow paused at a usage limit in the terminal to stay paused after a login, until the earlier login returns or you type a prompt
  • Fixed a nested claude with its own token being refused by forceLoginOrgUUID: commands that don't get the session's token no longer get its CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_SCOPES; set it on any that need it
  • Fixed headless sessions losing stored messages on resume when a message was sent again with the same UUID after the process was killed
  • Fixed cases where a session resumed after an empty reply or a killed command lost an answer, or brought back a rewound prompt, after another crash or a move to the background
  • Fixed a remote session forgetting messages sent after Stop was pressed during a restart, if Claude Code then crashed
  • Fixed tasks created after /clear being lost, and cleared tasks coming back, when a cloud or self-hosted runner session with no feature flags loaded resumed later
  • Fixed a compaction right after a reply cut at the output token limit losing that reply's tool call and its result
  • Fixed a settings change from /config and similar commands failing to save with no warning; a line under the prompt now says so
  • Fixed /rewind closing without a word when some files could not be restored
  • Fixed pasted images being dropped when the prompt starts with a file path such as /tmp/a.txt
  • Fixed agents passed with --agents being lost once plugins loaded or reloaded
  • Fixed a plugin's agent being dropped when resuming a session from the --resume picker
  • Fixed Claude Code refusing to start when https_proxy or HTTPS_PROXY is a bare host:port and neither its input nor its output is a terminal (the desktop app, an SDK, cron)
  • Fixed Claude Code on Linux sometimes returning to the shell while restarting itself at startup, such as after the first sign-in to a Claude apps gateway or when turning on Code Mode
  • Fixed claude -p hanging before its first request when the fetch of a model's settings stalled, such as at a proxy; it now goes on without them after 10 seconds
  • Fixed the screen staying blank or frozen after a brief out-of-memory error
  • Fixed a rare display fault that could freeze the screen or end the session
  • Fixed cloud sessions breaking when a program left thousands of connections open to the session's network proxy
  • Fixed a turn hanging when a mod's $.model.complete or $.model.classify call met a usage limit: the call now gets the API's error at once; mods should handle that error
  • Fixed stalls on a compaction reply with thousands of unclosed tags and on some very long WebFetch URLs; WebFetch now refuses a URL over 2,000 characters before any permission prompt
  • Fixed a message with thousands of @ mentions stalling before Claude replies; only the first 100 mentions are now looked up as files
  • Fixed the prompt freezing after rejecting a write to a very large file; a rejected write now shows a short preview
  • Fixed a crash when a burst of keys reached the search box in /plugin
  • Fixed a false crash report and exit code when a suspended session resumes, or at exit, where a Linux security policy blocks a process from signalling itself
  • Fixed remote MCP servers staying disconnected after a longer outage such as a VPN drop: most servers on other machines reached by hostname over https are now retried in the background for about a day
  • Fixed Edit refusing with "File has not been read yet" after a compaction on unchanged files outside the project that Claude had already read in full
  • Fixed Grep repeating or skipping results when paging with head_limit and offset; content and count results are now sorted by file path
  • Fixed Read failing on Jupyter notebooks that contain an output of an unknown type

  • Fixed the Read tool reporting 512KB instead of the real size when a file of 10 MB or more is too large to read at once

  • Fixed artifact publishes failing with "the source file changed between approval and publish" when a synced or remote-backed folder had only changed the file's timestamp

  • Fixed a Stop hook that failed to run being shown as having reported a problem

title: llm 0.37.3
summary:
Release: llm 0.37.3

A bug fix release for LLM, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software.

Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1, which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code.

Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL:

select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))

Returns this:

{"a":[1]}

But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this:

{"a":"[1]"}

According to D. Richard Hipp:

That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug.

The workaround looks like this:

select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1))))

title: Building strong safety evaluations
summary: Recommendations for designing, running, and reporting safety evaluations, based on our own experiences.
story_key: story|title:building strong safety evaluations
content_excerpt: Safety evaluations inform some of the most consequential decisions we make about an AI model, including whether it’s ready to deploy, which safeguards ship alongside it, and what our next round of safety training and research should focus on. When we say a model is “safer than its predecessor,” we mean that it scored better on a set of evals someone built. But a safety claim is only as sound as the eval behind it, and good ones are hard to build. A safety eval measures a model’s propensity to cause or contribute to harm, whether its response to a request makes harm more or less likely, and how severe that harm would be, rather than measuring specific capabilities. It can cover different types of harm. For example, a user may actively request harmful outputs (such as seeking instructions on how to harm themselves), or they may request outputs that are intended to be harmless, but that come with high risk of unintended harm (such as seeking information on the appropriate dose of a drug). Essentially, a safety eval asks, “Given a specific input, did the model do the right thing?” Like other types of evals, these can be tricky to get right: researchers have repeatedly found that AI evals are easy to game , don’t always measure what they claim to measure, and aren’t documented well enough to reproduce . The results can change depending on whether the questions are multiple-choice or open-ended , or even based on how answer options are ordered . Psychology faced similar issues a decade ago, when large-scale replication projects found that many published findings didn’t hold up, likely at least in part because many original studies relied on small samples and journals favored statistically significant results. In response, the field instituted reforms such as preregistration (writing down hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting or analyzing data), better measurement, and more rigorous statistics, which made measurements more trustworthy and results easier to replicate. Drawing on those reforms, and from our experience building evals at Anthropic , 1 this post shares recommendations for anyone who builds or relies on AI safety evaluations, using examples from our system cards . Building a strong safety eval requires multiple perspectives, including from subject-matter and technical experts. title: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
story_key: story|ver:4.1|title:llmon an llm native markup language now in granite 4 1 3b and 8b
content_excerpt: LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections. To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages. Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview . We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates. JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans. LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. title: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
story_key: story|title:xybench helping with the problem behind the question
content_excerpt: Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench , a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026. A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem : a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed. Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses. The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal. People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask. We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. title: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
summary: AlphaProof Code agents wrote three  million lines of proofs in Lean to verify Signal’s core encryption.
story_key: story|title:introducing alphaproof code a breakthrough in verifying complex software at dept
content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties – such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised – down to the exact code running on devices.
